topics.chapterTitle: Managing Configuration, Dependencies, and Service Lifecycle
topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: A service starts successfully with one configuration, then fails after a reload changes the queue limit while existing requests still use the old worker count. Another instance reports ready before opening its database. A third hangs during shutdown because a consumer waits on a queue whose producer has already been destroyed. These failures arise from lifecycle design, not from an exotic distributed algorithm.

topics.title: 4.1.1 Parsing Values with Units and Bounds
topics.summary: Configuration is an input language. It needs syntax, types, ranges, and error messages. A field named timeout is ambiguous unless its unit is defined. A queue capacity of zero may mean disabled, unlimited, or invalid in different libraries. The application must select one meaning rather than inherit an accidental default.

topics.title: 4.1.2 Establishing Precedence and Configuration Identity
topics.summary: Many applications combine defaults, files, environment variables, and command-line options. Define the precedence once and expose the effective nonsecret configuration for inspection. Otherwise an operator may edit a file that is silently overridden by an environment variable and conclude that the application ignored the change.

topics.title: 4.2.1 Using Immutable Snapshots
topics.summary: An immutable configuration snapshot lets a request observe one coherent policy throughout its lifetime. The application builds and validates a new snapshot, then replaces the current reference. Existing requests retain the old snapshot until they finish. This avoids a request seeing a new timeout but an old retry count halfway through processing.

topics.summary: A reload should have a commit point. Parse and validate a candidate outside the active configuration. If validation fails, preserve the previous snapshot and report the failure. Mutating active fields one by one can leave a mixed state when a later field is invalid.

blocks.text: The same principle applies to dependent resources. If a new endpoint requires a connection pool, construct and validate that pool before swapping it into service where practical. If construction fails, retain the old pool. If the resource cannot coexist with the old one, the operation is a disruptive transition and should be designed as such rather than hidden inside a “reload” function.

topics.title: 4.3.1 Starting Dependencies Before Advertising Readiness
topics.summary: Startup should follow dependency order. Construct validated configuration, open required stores, verify supported schema versions, initialize execution resources, bind the listener, and only then advertise the appropriate readiness state. The exact sequence depends on the service, but readiness must correspond to a defined useful capability.

cards.question: Explain Starting Dependencies Before Advertising Readiness in your own words.
cards.answer: Startup should follow dependency order. Construct validated configuration, open required stores, verify supported schema versions, initialize execution resources, bind the listener, and only then advertise the appropriate readiness state. The exact sequence depends on the service, but readiness must correspond to a defined useful capability.

reading.title: 4.3.1 Starting Dependencies Before Advertising Readiness
paragraphs: Startup should follow dependency order. Construct validated configuration, open required stores, verify supported schema versions, initialize execution resources, bind the listener, and only then advertise the appropriate readiness state. The exact sequence depends on the service, but readiness must correspond to a defined useful capability.

The gateway opens its API and dispatcher database connections before starting the dispatcher thread and printing its listening port. This reduces the chance that a “ready” process immediately discovers an unusable database. The printed READY line is a lab synchronization signal, not a production readiness endpoint or proof that the remote worker is available.

A gateway that can durably accept work during a worker outage may reasonably report submission readiness while reporting delivery degradation separately. A service that cannot safely accept any work without the dependency should not report that same readiness. Readiness is a contract for a particular operation, not a universal property inferred from process existence.

Partial startup must unwind safely. RAII releases resources that were successfully acquired. A thread that starts before a later constructor fails must be stopped and joined before captured state is destroyed. Resource declaration order and exception paths deserve the same review as the happy path.

blocks.text: A stop token is cooperative. It does not forcibly interrupt arbitrary blocking code. Every blocking operation in the shutdown path needs a strategy: a deadline, a wakeup mechanism, a close operation with defined semantics, or a documented external termination policy. Joining a thread that waits forever on an unclosed queue can make graceful shutdown impossible.

blocks.text: Signal handlers are especially constrained. The companion’s handler only stores to an atomic stop flag whose lock-free property is checked at compile time. It does not allocate, log through iostreams, lock a mutex, or close random application objects. The ordinary control flow observes the flag and performs the actual shutdown. This keeps asynchronous signal context separate from normal resource management. A relaxed atomic is sufficient for this notification because it publishes no other data; it also permits safe observation when a signal is delivered on a different thread. The handler relies on the specific allowance for plain lock-free atomic operations, not on a claim that every atomic or library call is signal-safe. (R48)

topics.title: Failure clinic — Joining the Consumer Before Closing the Queue
topics.summary: A service owns a queue, a producer, and a consumer. During shutdown it joins the producer, then joins the consumer, then closes the queue. If the consumer is waiting for another item, the second join never completes. The close operation that would wake it lies after the blocked join.

blocks.text: The fix is to define terminal queue state and place the close before waiting for consumers to finish. If accepted items must drain, pop() returns queued values after close and returns no value only once the queue is empty. If cancellation discards items, report that separate policy explicitly. Do not call both behaviors “close” without explaining which one applies.
